transcript.content: Hello, please have a seat. What brings you into the clinic today?

Hi. Thank you. Um, I'm here because... well, I just can't seem to shake this feeling that work isn't safe anymore. And I just feel like I'm somehow damaged now. Like the competent person who got promoted just... isn't really there anymore.
Did something specific happen at work that made you start feeling unsafe?
Yeah, there was. Um, this has all been going on since a break-in that happened at the office. I was working an overnight deployment when it happened... that was about two years and four months ago.
Do unwanted memories or images of the break-in keep popping into your mind?

Yeah, they do. It doesn't really take much to set it off, either. Just hearing a badge scanner beep, or... heavy footsteps in the hallway, or even getting a late-night deployment alert on my phone. It can suddenly put me right back in that office. My chest gets really tight, and the image of the guard on the floor just... it just cuts right through whatever I’m trying to do at the time.
Do you find yourself actively avoiding thoughts, places, or reminders connected to the break-in?

Yeah, I definitely do. I've actually started trading shifts, or... pushing back on our release windows so I don't have to be there at night. And if I do have to go to the office, I always take the side entrance, or I just try to work from home whenever I can. Just... walking through that main lobby after dark makes me feel like I’m going to come apart, so I do whatever I can to avoid it.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets diagnostic criteria for Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (F43.1) following exposure to a traumatic workplace break-in occurring over two years ago. Presentation includes recurrent intrusive distressing memories triggered by trauma-related cues, physiological reactivity, active avoidance of trauma-related reminders and situations (e.g., night shifts, main lobby), persistent negative changes in self-perception ('damaged'), and occupational/functional impairment lasting well beyond one month.

confirmed_symptoms: Recurrent, involuntary, and intrusive distressing memories and images of the break-in and injured guard
Physiological reactivity and feeling transported back to the event upon exposure to trauma-related cues
Avoidance of external reminders including working night shifts and entering through the main lobby after dark
Altering work patterns (trading shifts, working from home) to avoid trauma triggers
Persistent negative beliefs about oneself (feeling damaged and changed)
Persistent sense of threat and lack of safety

diagnostic_checklist.duration_verified: Symptoms have persisted for approximately 2 years and 4 months since the traumatic break-in.
additional_requirements: Symptoms not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance or another medical condition
